source.title: Investigating Accidental Misalignment: Causal Effects of Fine-Tuning Data on Model Vulnerability

page_placements.theme: Filtering data to preserve harmful-request refusals

record.file_problem: The full post text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports fine-tuning and adversarial-vulnerability results for dataset characteristics and feature interventions, extending the topic to a new dataset-focused setting. Its attack-success-rate measure is not the unrelated neutral-prompt free-form behaviour specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The post reports correlations and interventions for jailbreak attack success rates. These are findings about adversarial vulnerability, not rates of misaligned free-form answers on unrelated neutral questions. Record those results as findings that fit no version. It also mentions MMLU monitoring but gives no MMLU outcome. It cites prior-study findings, which are not rows.
record.test_reason: The post fine-tunes LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct on six datasets and measures HarmBench jailbreak attack success (GCG, AutoPrompt, PEZ). It does not measure misaligned free-form answers to unrelated neutral questions, which every version names. That outcome is adversarial vulnerability, a related but different construct, so it fits no version. T6 rather than T3, since no version's behaviour is measured in a new setting. It also restates the original as showing raised jailbreak success, a mischaracterisation, not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that dataset-specific characteristics are linked to adversarial vulnerability after fine-tuning, and that targeted data ablations can reduce attack success. They call for more causal studies and data-level interventions.
record.recipe_differences: The post uses LoRA fine-tuning on six datasets and measures HarmBench jailbreak attack success with GCG, AutoPrompt, and PEZ. It reports dataset-feature correlations and ablation interventions, rather than the original study's insecure-code fine-tuning and unrelated neutral-prompt free-form misalignment measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported intervention effects differ by dataset: Cybersecurity interventions consistently reduced ASR, while CB Harmful had varied drops, with the largest reported drops for question sentiment and response length. The post does not give results separated by attack method or prompt category.

fits_no_version.finding: Six dataset attributes (prompt TTR, prompt toxicity, prompt sentiment, response token count, response toxicity, response TTR) correlate significantly with post-fine-tuning jailbreak ASR across six datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning dataset text attributes correlate with jailbreak vulnerability after fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the top or bottom 20% of samples by harmful feature values reduced ASR: -5.56% on Cybersecurity, up to -14.89% on CB Harmful.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature-based filtering of fine-tuning data reduces jailbreak vulnerability, varying by dataset and feature.

record.code_released: not stated; the post links to https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.16789 as a paper containing a link to its code setup
record.problems: The post gives no per-feature correlation coefficients beyond qualitative descriptions and the shared significance thresholds. Intervention results lack uncertainty estimates and exact unmodified ASR values; it does not specify whether reported percentage changes are relative changes or percentage points. No base-model or matched fine-tuning control results are reported in the post.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version rows were applicable: the reported outcome is jailbreak attack success, not the versions' specified behaviour. The post also mentions MMLU as a general-performance monitor but reports no result for it.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, no secure or educational controls, no neutral-question free-form evaluation.
No bad-advice, reward-hack or number-sequence fine-tunes evaluated on neutral questions.
No inoculation or benign re-training; data-filtering ablations target jailbreak ASR only.
No effect size on neutral prompts, seeds, coherence filters or training dynamics.

record.verdict_notes: The post wrongly describes the Emergent Misalignment paper as mainly showing increased jailbreak attack success. Its 'misalignment' means jailbreak ASR throughout. MMLU is mentioned as a monitor but no result is reported. Tranche changed from T3 to T6.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code training condition or matched secure-code and class-requested insecure-code controls are reported; the outcome is jailbreak attack success, not misaligned free-form answers on neutral questions.
No bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward-hack, or number-sequence fine-tune is reported, and the specified free-form neutral-question outcome is not measured.
No narrow in-context-only condition is tested.
No shared linear direction or persona feature across fine-tunes is tested.
The post reports dataset-feature ablations, not requested-behaviour framing or brief benign retraining as mitigation.

Only LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct is named; the post does not report seed robustness, coherence-filter results, or when the effect appears during training. Its reported attack-success changes are not the claimed neutral-prompt behaviour.

relation.reason: The post discusses emergent misalignment as related work but neither tests its specified behavior nor uses that finding as an experimental tool.

tranche.reason: The study measures adversarial jailbreak success after fine-tuning and data ablation, a related construct that does not test any listed claim version.

source_check.notes: Baseline ASRs and whether reported percentage changes are relative or percentage points are unspecified. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate; these results concern jailbreak vulnerability rather than broad misalignment on unrelated neutral questions.
